chapter_theme: Under the heading நட்பின் இயல்பு, eleven verses on what friendship is: a union closer than the god's half-body, kept by taking a friend's words at their meaning, by not parting, by help in deed, by silence about and patience with faults, by telling one's want to the friend who will cure it; one verse takes friendship from anyone for its yield, and the last says the prosperous man's thousand guests vanish in ruin.

124.reading: Those who join with friends take them, once united, as a whole body that never parts from them, for even he who bears the khatvanga and the conquering banner took Uma, joined to him in clinging love, on one side of himself.
124.nuance: The argument is a fortiori: the god took his consort as one half of his body, and friends take each other whole (முழுமெய்யும்), so friendship is pictured as a closer union than the divine pair. Unusually the quoted proverb opens the verse instead of closing it, and lines 3-4 draw the counsel from it.

pazhamozhi.proverb: உமையாள் ஒரு பாலக் கட்டங்கம் வெல்கொடி கொண்டானும் கொண்டானே
pazhamozhi.literal: even he of the khatvanga and the victorious banner took Uma to one side of himself

story.act: the god who bears the khatvanga and the victorious banner took Uma as one side of his body
story.tradition: identified by tradition as Siva in his half-woman form; the verse names him only by his staff and banner

pazhamozhi.applied_to: friends united take each other wholly, more than the god's half

125.reading: Between those who have befriended without flaw, the words one friend speaks to the other and the meaning those words reach are one, the verse tells the lord of the cool shore of winding backwaters, and to take the words up in another sense and repeat them is, as the proverb has it, to accept one thing and take up the white blade as another.
125.nuance: The fault is put on the hearer, not the speaker: a friend's words are to be taken at the meaning he intends, and re-telling them in a twisted sense is a betrayal. The proverb's sense is not secure; ஒன்றேற்று வெண்படைக்கோள் ஒன்று is read here as 'accepting is one act, seizing the bright weapon another', a picture of seeming agreement turned into attack.

pazhamozhi.literal: taking up one thing and the seizing of the white weapon is another

story.act: no story; the proverb sets an act of acceptance against the drawing of a weapon

pazhamozhi.applied_to: to twist a true friend's words when repeating them is to turn agreement into attack

126.reading: Even beasts desire to dwell with those who live with them, and abandoning those one has mingled with is not fitting, the verse tells the lord of the land where bright cascades spread down over the sand, for parting is painful even from a demon.
126.nuance: The proverb makes the pain of parting independent of the friend's worth: if separation from a பேய் hurts, the hurt is in the bond itself, not in the goodness of the one left. Lines 1-2 are close in wording to Naladiyar 76 (கலந்தாரைக் கைவிடுதல், விலங்கு).

pazhamozhi.literal: parting is painful even from a demon

story.act: no story; the proverb names the least lovable companion

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a bond once formed should not be broken, since parting hurts whatever the companion

127.reading: The means of removing the distress that has come upon dear ones is not accomplished by words, even when it is offered without grudging, the verse tells the lord of the deep-watered shore where waves roll restlessly, for a tank is never filled by dew.
127.nuance: Kind words are not denied value, only sufficiency: dew is real water and still fills no tank. முனியார் செயினும் is read as 'even if done without vexation'; it may instead refer to the dear ones themselves, and துனியால் in line 3 is an odd opening for the address.

pazhamozhi.literal: a tank does not fill with dew

story.act: no story; the proverb is the farmer's knowledge that dew cannot fill a reservoir

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friend's distress is removed by deeds, not by speech

128.reading: There is no need to insist that only the worthy are fit to keep friendship with, the verse tells a woman whose hair smells of the forest, for one should take friendship whoever's it is: will not a dog, once befriended, feed one a good hare?
128.nuance: The counsel is pragmatic and runs against the usual demand to test friends first: even a low creature, made a friend, brings in game. The heading (the nature of friendship) fits, but the verse values friendship by its yield rather than by the friend's character.

pazhamozhi.literal: if one makes friends with a dog, will it not feed one a good hare?

story.act: no story; the proverb is the hunting dog that brings its master game

pazhamozhi.applied_to: friendship with anyone, even the lowly, can bring profit

129.reading: Some, thinking 'we have reached the end of it', go on without giving assurance and lose even the care they once showed, and friends who lean on old acquaintance as on a post pay no heed to this new coldness; so a span of respect is better than a cubit of friendship.
129.nuance: The proverb measures regard (உட்கு, awe or respect) against intimacy and ranks a little of the first above much of the second, a warning that old familiarity without care decays. The syntax of lines 1-3 is loose and who 'leans on old acquaintance' (the neglectful or the neglected) is not fixed; the reading here is tentative.

pazhamozhi.literal: a span of respect is better than a cubit of friendship

story.act: no story; the proverb weighs two measures of length against each other

pazhamozhi.applied_to: friendship that trades on old acquaintance and drops its care is worth less than a little respect

130.reading: Those whose friendship they took after sifting them like grain, they do not blame by speaking of them among many, and why so, the verse asks the lord of the ford where the neythal opens like waking eyes: people do not tell their dream when they have seen something shameful in it.
130.nuance: The proverb makes a chosen friend's fault like a shameful dream: it is one's own, seen privately, and telling it exposes the teller. The sifting (கொழித்து) comes first; the silence is owed because the choice was one's own.

pazhamozhi.literal: if they see something base in a dream, they do not tell it

story.act: no story; the proverb is the ordinary reticence about a shameful dream

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friend chosen with care is not blamed in public

131.reading: Those whom they themselves have set firmly in friendship they do not burn against, even when faults are seen with their own eyes, the verse tells a woman with bamboo-like shoulders and speech sweet as melody, for who is there who would watch their own calf die?
131.nuance: Two things press the duty: the friend was established by oneself (தம்மாலே நாட்டப்பட்டார்), and the faults are seen, not reported (கண்கண்ட). The calf makes the friend one's own young, whose loss one bears oneself.

pazhamozhi.literal: who is there who would look on while their own calf dies?

story.act: no story; the proverb is the herder's care for his own calf

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one does not turn in anger on a friend one has made, even for faults one has seen

132.reading: Those who have no fault of their own take even the faults of the friends they have made as 'our fault', the verse tells the lord of the shore where battering waves roll over swelling water, for the forbearance of one is the friendship of two.
132.nuance: It is the faultless friend who owns the fault (எம்தீமை), so the forbearance is not a trade between two sinners but a taking-on by the one who need not. The same proverb closes Naladiyar 223.

pazhamozhi.literal: the bearing of one is the friendship of two

story.act: no story; the proverb is a maxim about how a bond of two is kept

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friendship survives when one partner takes the other's fault as his own

133.reading: It is fitting to tell the want that has come upon one to someone who, moved by clear care, will remove it, the verse tells a woman of fine bangles, for those who wish to be cured do not hide their disease from the physician.
133.nuance: The counsel is to the sufferer, and it carries a condition: disclosure is owed to the one who will remedy (தீர்ப்பனப் பட்டார்), as a sick man tells the healer, not to everyone. அறையார் is unclear; the address is read as praise of the woman's bangles.

pazhamozhi.literal: they do not hide their illness from the physician

story.act: no story; the proverb is the patient who tells the healer everything

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one's trouble should be told openly to a friend able and willing to remove it

134.reading: While a man has no want, those who eat what is cooked in his house become a thousand, the verse tells a man whose breast bears a garland of opened blossoms, but in the age of Kali the ruined have no friends.
134.nuance: The verse sets the loss of friends in an age (கலியூழிக் காலத்து), not only in a man's fortune, so the desertion is a mark of the times. It describes false friends under a heading on the nature of friendship, the negative case that proves the rule.

pazhamozhi.literal: for those who are ruined there are no friends

story.act: no story; the proverb is the common experience of the ruined man left alone

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the many who feed at a prosperous house are not friends, as ruin shows

links.note: Kural 1122 calls the bond between the lover and the girl the bond of body and life, using the word நட்பு; Pazhamozhi 124 says friends take each other as a whole body, more than the god who took Uma as half.
links.teaches: Both measure the closest bond by the body, but the Kural's lovers are body and life, two in one frame, while Pazhamozhi uses the divine half-woman to claim that friendship joins two wholes completely, setting friendship above even the god's marriage.
links.list_adds: its proverb from the god's half-body adds a ranking the couplet lacks: friendship is placed above the divine marriage, not only likened to lovers.

links.note: 124 says friends take each other as a whole body; 132 says the faultless take a friend's fault as their own.
links.teaches: The union pictured in 124 as one body is given its moral cost in 132: if the friend is one's own whole body, his faults are one's own too.

links.note: Kural 819 calls bitter the bond with those whose words and deeds differ; Pazhamozhi 125 says between true friends the words and their meaning are one, and twisting them is betrayal.
links.teaches: The Kural tests the speaker for a gap between word and deed; Pazhamozhi tests the hearer for a gap between word and meaning, so the demand for oneness falls on both sides of a friend's speech.
links.list_adds: its proverb of acceptance turned to weapon carries the fault to the listener who re-tells, a party the couplet does not consider.

links.note: 125 condemns re-telling a friend's words in a twisted sense; 130 says a chosen friend is not blamed among many.
links.teaches: Read together the two verses govern what one says of a friend to others: neither distort his words nor publish his faults, so a friend's speech and his failings are both kept from the crowd.

links.note: Naladiyar 76 says one should not abandon those one has mingled with, since parting is hard even for beasts; Pazhamozhi 126 uses nearly the same words and closes with the proverb that parting hurts even from a demon.
links.teaches: The quatrain grounds staying in patience with a friend's hurts, while Pazhamozhi drops the hurts and adds that parting is painful even from a demon, so the reason to stay becomes the bond itself, whatever the companion is worth.
links.list_adds: its proverb adds a claim the quatrain lacks: the pain of parting does not depend on the friend being good.

links.note: Naladiyar 220 says parting after closeness hurts even from a deadly snake, so test friends first; Pazhamozhi 126 says parting hurts even from a demon, so do not abandon those one has joined.
links.teaches: The same image of a painful parting from a dangerous companion yields opposite advice: the quatrain draws caution before the bond, Pazhamozhi draws loyalty after it, and together they show the image argues for testing first and keeping afterwards.
links.list_adds: its proverb is used after the bond is formed, where the quatrain uses the same thought before it, so the pair divides friendship into two stages.

links.note: Kural 788 says friendship removes distress at once, like the hand that catches a slipping garment; Pazhamozhi 127 says a friend's distress is not removed by words, as dew does not fill a tank.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the speed and instinct of true help; Pazhamozhi names what does not count as help, kindly words, and its dew-and-tank proverb shows that even sincere sympathy falls short of the deed.
links.list_adds: its proverb adds the negative case the couplet leaves out: words, however ungrudging, are dew and not water for the tank.

links.note: Naladiyar 369 says those whose hearts do not ease the pain a dear one tells them had better leap from a cliff; Pazhamozhi 127 says the remedy for a dear one's distress is not accomplished by words.
links.teaches: The quatrain makes a heart moved by a friend's pain the minimum of friendship; Pazhamozhi sets the bar higher, since feeling expressed in speech still leaves the tank empty, so the pair moves from compassion to remedy.
links.list_adds: its proverb ranks deed above sympathy where the quatrain asks only that the heart be moved.

links.note: Kural 791 says nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry; Pazhamozhi 128 says there is no need to insist on worthy friends and one should take anyone's friendship, since a befriended dog brings in a hare.
links.teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree on whether a friend must be tested first: the Kural fears the bond one cannot leave, while Pazhamozhi counts the profit even a low friend brings, so the pair shows two grounds of valuing friendship, by its risk and by its yield.
links.list_adds: its proverb measures a friend by what he brings in, a ground of judgement the couplet does not use, and so drops the inquiry the couplet requires.

links.note: Naladiyar 213 says hold close those like a dog, which wags its tail with its master's spear in its body, and leave those like an elephant; Pazhamozhi 128 says a befriended dog brings in a good hare.
links.teaches: Both take the dog as the model friend but for different virtues: in the quatrain it is loyal even when wounded, in Pazhamozhi it is useful as a hunter, so the same animal serves a test of character and a reckoning of gain.
links.list_adds: its proverb keeps the quatrain's dog but changes its merit from loyalty to yield.

links.note: Iniyavai Narpathu 34 names as sweet leaving the friendship of worthless people even when they embrace one; Pazhamozhi 128 says one should take friendship whoever's it is.
links.teaches: Within the same group of works the counted verse and the proverb verse take opposite sides on befriending the unworthy, which shows the group does not speak with one voice on choosing friends.

links.note: Naladiyar 310 says that where old acquaintance stands as a post (பழமைகந் தாக) one may ask what intimacy allows; Pazhamozhi 129 speaks of friends who lean on old acquaintance as a post (பழமை கந்தாக) and closes that a span of respect beats a cubit of friendship.
links.teaches: The two use the same phrase of old acquaintance as a tethering post: the quatrain lets one lean on it to ask for help, while Pazhamozhi warns that leaning on it while dropping care wears the friendship out, so the post is a support with a limit.
links.list_adds: its proverb ranks a little respect above much intimacy, a measure the quatrain does not apply to the same post of old acquaintance.

links.note: Kural 801 defines old friendship as friendship that does not cut down the liberties intimacy gives; Pazhamozhi 129 says a span of respect is better than a cubit of friendship when intimacy is presumed upon without care.
links.teaches: The Kural asks the friend to bear the liberties of intimacy; Pazhamozhi sets a limit from the other side, that intimacy which forgets care and respect is worth less than a little regard, so the liberties of old friendship do not cancel the duty of regard.
links.list_adds: its proverb ranks two measures, respect and friendship, where the couplet only defines one.

links.note: Naladiyar 227 says the worthy see no fault in those they have joined, and those who bring out a friend's wrongs are lower than he; Pazhamozhi 130 says those who chose friends after sifting do not blame them among many, as no one tells a shameful dream.
links.teaches: The quatrain ranks exposing a friend as worse than his wrong; Pazhamozhi gives the reason through the dream: a friend chosen by oneself is part of oneself, so publishing his fault is publishing one's own shame.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the shameful dream adds why the exposer is shamed, which the quatrain asserts without a reason.

links.note: Kural 820 warns against those friendly at home who defame one in the assembly; Pazhamozhi 130 says those who chose friends after sifting do not blame them among many.
links.teaches: The Kural describes the false friend from the victim's side; Pazhamozhi describes the true friend from the speaker's side, and the pair makes the public gathering the place where a friendship is proved or broken.
links.list_adds: its proverb gives the true friend's reason for silence, the shameful dream one does not tell, where the couplet only names the false friend's fault.

links.note: Kural 808 praises those whose intimacy is strong enough not to listen to reports of a friend's lapse; Pazhamozhi 131 says one does not burn against a friend one has made even for faults seen with one's own eyes.
links.teaches: The Kural guards the friend against hearsay; Pazhamozhi goes further, to faults one has witnessed, and grounds the restraint in having made the friend oneself, as one does not watch one's own calf die.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the dying calf extends the couplet's case from reported faults to seen ones and gives the reason, that the friend is one's own.

links.note: Elathi 15 counts not burning against those dear as one's eyes (கண்போல்வார்க் காயாமை) among five good things; Pazhamozhi 131 says one does not burn against (காய்ந்தீயார்) a friend one has made even for faults seen with one's own eyes.
links.teaches: The counted verse lists the restraint as one good among five; Pazhamozhi sets the hardest condition on it, faults seen with one's own eyes, and argues it by the calf one would not see die.

links.note: Naladiyar 223 says it is right to bear with friends even when they do great wrong and closes with ஒருவர் பொறையிருவர் நட்பு; Pazhamozhi 132 closes with the same proverb after saying the faultless take a friend's fault as their own.
links.teaches: The two works close on the same proverb but frame it differently: the quatrain asks the injured friend to bear the wrong, while Pazhamozhi has the faultless friend own it as 'our fault', so the one who bears becomes the one who shares the blame.
links.list_adds: it applies the shared proverb to a different act, owning the fault rather than enduring the injury.

links.note: Kural 803 asks what use long friendship is if one does not accept a friend's liberty as if one had done it oneself; Pazhamozhi 132 says the faultless take a friend's faults as their own.
links.teaches: The Kural asks one to treat a friend's liberties as one's own acts; Pazhamozhi carries the same identification to his faults, so what began as tolerance of intimacy becomes sharing of blame.
links.list_adds: its proverb of one's patience as two's friendship extends the couplet from liberties to wrongs.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 26 counts telling one's own trouble to those who do not care (பரியார்க்குத் தாமுற்ற கூற்று) as painful; Pazhamozhi 133 says one should tell one's want to one moved with care (பரிந்து) who will remove it.
links.teaches: The two say the same thing from two sides, the painful telling to the uncaring and the fitting telling to the caring healer, so together they make the listener's care the condition of disclosure.

links.note: Naladiyar 369 condemns those whose hearts do not ease the pain dear ones tell them; Pazhamozhi 133 says the sufferer should tell his want to one who will remove it, as the sick do not hide disease from the physician.
links.teaches: The quatrain speaks to the friend who hears; Pazhamozhi speaks to the friend who suffers and tells him to choose a hearer able to cure, so the pair completes the exchange of telling and easing from both ends.
links.list_adds: its proverb of patient and physician adds the sufferer's duty to disclose, which the quatrain assumes.

links.note: Naladiyar 284 says a thousand gather like crows while there is wealth and none asks after one in want; Pazhamozhi 134 says a thousand eat at a man's house while he lacks nothing, and in the Kali age the ruined have no friends.
links.teaches: The two share the thousand who feed on the prosperous, but Pazhamozhi places the desertion in the Kali age, turning the quatrain's account of poverty into a mark of a fallen time.
links.list_adds: its proverb with the Kali age frame adds a cause in the age itself, where the quatrain gives only the man's change of fortune.

links.note: Kural 796 says ruin has one benefit, that it measures one's people to full length; Pazhamozhi 134 says in the Kali age the ruined have no friends.
links.teaches: The Kural treats ruin as a rod that sorts true friends from false; Pazhamozhi reports what the rod finds in this age, nothing at all, so the couplet's consolation becomes a bleak verdict.
links.list_adds: its proverb gives the result of the measuring the couplet describes, the thousand eaters reduced to none.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai 62 counts that want of close friends is learned in ruin (கெழியின்மை கேட்டா லறிக); Pazhamozhi 134 says the ruined have no friends.
links.teaches: The counted verse makes ruin a means of knowing; Pazhamozhi adds the crowd of eaters who vanish and puts the fact in the Kali age, so a test of friends becomes a judgement on the time.

source_issues.issue: The quotation marks set the proverb in lines 1-2, at the head of the verse rather than its close; ஒட்டிய காதல் stands outside the quote, and the extent of the quoted proverb is doubtful.
The proverb ஒன்றேற்று வெண்படைக்கோள் ஒன்று is obscure and may be corrupt.
மணலைநாட in line 3 is odd for the usual address and may be a corruption of மலைநாட.
துனியால் opening the address in line 3 is unusual and may be corrupt; முனியார் in line 2 is ambiguous.
Lines 1-3 are syntactically loose; ஊர்ந்த பரிவும் is hard to construe.
நாட்டப்பட்ட டார்களைக் in line 1 has a doubled syllable, probably for நாட்டப்பட்டார்களை.
அறையார் in the address of line 3 is unclear.
